questions.q: Which two layers make up the skin itself?
options: The papillary layer and the reticular layer
questions.why: The skin proper has two layers: the epidermis, a thin superficial layer of epithelium, and the dermis, a thicker connective tissue layer beneath it. The hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) lies deep to the dermis and anchors the skin to underlying structures, but it is not counted as part of the skin. Keeping this boundary in mind helps when you later sort injection depths and burn depths.
notes: The epidermis is part of the skin, but the hypodermis is the fatty layer beneath the skin and is not part of it. Pick this pairing only if the question asked for the outermost and innermost layers a needle crosses before reaching muscle.
The papillary and reticular layers are the two layers of the dermis only. They would be the answer if the question asked for the two layers of the dermis, not of the whole skin.
Correct. The epidermis on top and the dermis beneath it are the two layers of the skin proper.
The dermis is part of the skin, but the hypodermis lies below the skin. This pairing would fit a question asking which two layers sit deep to the epidermis.

questions.q: Which layer of the skin is the superficial layer?
questions.why: The epidermis is the superficial (surface) layer of the skin. It is made of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and has no blood vessels of its own. The dermis lies directly beneath it, and the hypodermis lies deeper still, below the skin proper.
notes: The reticular layer is the deep part of the dermis, so it is one of the deepest parts of the skin. Choose it if the question asked which dermal layer lies closest to the hypodermis.
The hypodermis is the fatty subcutaneous layer below the skin, not a layer of the skin itself. It would be the answer for the layer that anchors the skin and stores fat.
The dermis is the deeper of the two skin layers, made of connective tissue that holds vessels, nerves, and glands. Pick it if the question asked for the deep layer of the skin.
Correct. The epidermis forms the outer surface of the skin.

questions.q: Which tissue makes up the epidermis?
questions.why: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Stratified means many layers of cells, squamous means the surface cells are flat, and keratinized means those surface cells are dead and packed with the tough protein keratin. This build lets the epidermis take constant wear while the deeper cells keep dividing to replace what is lost.
notes: Areolar connective tissue is the loose tissue of the papillary layer of the dermis. Pick it if the question asked what tissue forms the superficial dermis.
Adipose tissue is fat, and it makes up most of the hypodermis beneath the skin. Choose it if the question asked about the subcutaneous layer.
Correct. The epidermis is a layered epithelium whose flat surface cells are filled with keratin.
Dense irregular connective tissue makes up the reticular layer, the deep bulk of the dermis. It would be the answer for the tissue that gives the skin its strength.

questions.q: Which layer lies beneath the skin and is made mostly of adipose tissue?
questions.why: The hypodermis, also called the subcutaneous layer, lies deep to the dermis and is made of adipose and areolar connective tissue. It stores fat and anchors the skin to the fascia around muscles and bones. Although it sits right under the skin, it is not part of the skin itself.
notes: Correct. The hypodermis is the fatty subcutaneous layer deep to the dermis.

The reticular layer is the deep part of the dermis, made of dense irregular connective tissue with thick collagen bundles. It would be right for the dermal layer that gives skin its strength, not the fatty layer below the skin.
The deep fascia is a sheet of dense connective tissue wrapping muscles, deep to the hypodermis. Choose it if the question asked what the hypodermis anchors the skin to.

The dermis is the deep layer of the skin proper, made mostly of dense irregular connective tissue rather than fat. Pick it if the question asked which skin layer holds the vessels, nerves, and glands.

questions.q: Which stratum of the epidermis is the deepest?
questions.why: The stratum basale is the deepest stratum, a single row of cells resting on the basement membrane right above the dermis. These cells divide to produce new keratinocytes, which are pushed upward through the other strata. The course mnemonic Baby Screams Grandpa Loves Coffee lists the strata from deep to superficial: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum.
notes: The stratum corneum is the most superficial stratum, made of flat dead keratinized cells. Pick it if the question asked which stratum forms the surface.
The stratum granulosum sits in the middle of the epidermis, above the spinosum. It would be the answer if the question asked which stratum lies just deep to the lucidum in thick skin.
Correct. The stratum basale is the deepest stratum and the site of cell division.
The stratum spinosum lies directly on top of the basale, so students often mistake it for the deepest layer. Choose it if the question asked which stratum is just superficial to the basale.

questions.q: Which stratum forms the surface of the epidermis?
questions.why: The stratum corneum is the outermost stratum, made of many layers of flat, dead cells filled with keratin. These cells form a tough, water-resistant barrier and are constantly shed and replaced from below. In thick skin the corneum is much thicker, which is the main reason thick skin is thick.
notes: The stratum lucidum is a thin, clear layer just deep to the corneum, found only in thick skin. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer sits right under the surface layer on the palms and soles.
The stratum granulosum lies in the middle of the epidermis, where cells begin to die and fill with keratin. Choose it if the question asked which stratum lies just under the corneum in thin skin.
The stratum basale is the deepest stratum, where new cells are made. Pick it if the question asked where keratinocytes are born.
Correct. The stratum corneum is the dead, keratinized surface layer.

questions.q: Which epidermal cell produces keratin, the tough protective protein of the epidermis?
questions.why: Keratinocytes make up about 90 percent of epidermal cells and produce keratin, a tough fibrous protein that protects the skin from abrasion, heat, microbes, and chemicals. They also make lamellar granules, which release a water-repellent sealant. As keratinocytes move toward the surface they fill with keratin and die, forming the stratum corneum.
notes: Intraepidermal macrophages (Langerhans cells) come from red bone marrow and take part in immune responses against microbes in the skin. Choose them if the question asked about immune defense in the epidermis.
Correct. Keratinocytes are the most numerous epidermal cells and they make keratin.
Melanocytes produce melanin, the pigment that colors skin and absorbs UV light. Pick them if the question asked about pigment.
Tactile (Merkel) cells sit in the deepest layer of the epidermis and contact a sensory nerve ending for touch. They would be the answer for the touch-related epidermal cell.

questions.q: Which epidermal cell produces melanin?
questions.why: Melanocytes make melanin, a yellow-red or brown-black pigment that contributes to skin color and absorbs damaging UV light. They have long slender projections that pass melanin granules to nearby keratinocytes. Inside the keratinocytes, the melanin gathers over the nucleus and shields the DNA.
notes: Tactile (Merkel) cells contact a sensory nerve ending to detect touch. Choose them if the question asked which epidermal cell takes part in sensation.
Intraepidermal macrophages (Langerhans cells) are immune cells that help the body recognize invading microbes. They would be the answer for an immune question, not a pigment question.
Keratinocytes receive melanin from melanocytes but do not make it; they make keratin. Pick them if the question asked which cell produces keratin or stores the transferred pigment.
Correct. Melanocytes produce melanin and transfer it to keratinocytes.

questions.q: Which layer of the dermis is the superficial layer?
questions.why: The dermis has two layers. The papillary layer is the thin superficial layer, about one fifth of the dermis, and it pushes up into the epidermis as dermal papillae. The reticular layer is the thicker deep layer that makes up about four fifths of the dermis.
notes: Correct. The papillary layer is the superficial part of the dermis, just under the epidermis.
The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is not part of the skin. Choose it if the question asked for the fatty layer under the skin.
The reticular layer is the deep, thick layer of the dermis made of dense irregular connective tissue. Pick it if the question asked for the deep dermal layer.
The stratum basale is the deepest stratum of the epidermis, sitting just above the papillary layer. It would be the answer for the deepest epidermal layer, not a dermal layer.

questions.q: What is the onion-shaped, expanded base of a hair follicle called?
questions.why: The hair bulb is the onion-shaped expansion at the base of each follicle. It holds the hair matrix, a layer of dividing cells that grows the hair, and it surrounds the papilla of the hair, a small knob of connective tissue with blood vessels that nourish the matrix. Damage to the bulb stops hair growth from that follicle.
notes: The hair root is the part of the hair buried in the dermis inside the follicle. It would be the answer for the part of the hair below the skin surface, not the expanded base.
Correct. The hair bulb is the swollen base of the follicle where growth happens.
The papilla of the hair is the knob of areolar connective tissue and blood vessels that sits inside the bulb. Choose it if the question asked what supplies blood to the growing hair.
The hair shaft is the part of the hair that projects above the skin surface. Pick it if the question asked which part of the hair you can see.

questions.q: Which part of a nail contains the dividing cells that produce new nail?
questions.why: The nail matrix is epithelium at the proximal end of the nail, near the nail root, and it contains dividing cells that produce new nail cells. As new cells form, the nail is pushed forward over the fingertip. Damage to the matrix can permanently change or stop nail growth.
notes: The lunula is the whitish crescent at the proximal end of the nail body, pale because the epithelium there is thickened. Students confuse it with the matrix because it lies close to it, but the lunula is part of the visible nail.
Correct. The nail matrix is the growth region where new nail cells are made.
The hyponychium is thickened stratum corneum beneath the free edge that secures the nail to the fingertip. It would be the answer for the structure under the free edge.
The nail body is the visible plate of hard keratin. Pick it if the question asked which part of the nail you can see and paint.

questions.q: Which gland secretes sebum, an oily secretion?
questions.why: Sebaceous glands are the oil glands of the skin. Their secretory portion sits in the dermis, and most of their ducts open into a hair follicle, so the sebum coats the hair and skin. Sebum is a mixture of triglycerides, cholesterol, proteins, and salts that helps keep hair and skin from drying out.
notes: Eccrine sweat glands release watery sweat directly onto the skin surface to help cool the body. Pick them if the question asked about the most numerous sweat glands.

Apocrine sweat glands release a thicker sweat with lipids and proteins into hair follicles of the axillae and groin. Choose them if the question asked about sweat glands that become active at puberty.
Correct. Sebaceous glands secrete oily sebum, mostly into hair follicles.
Ceruminous glands secrete cerumen (earwax) into the external auditory canal. They would be the answer for a question about the ear canal.

questions.q: Which organ is the largest in the body by weight?
questions.why: The skin is the largest organ in the body by weight. In an adult it covers roughly 22 square feet and weighs about 10 to 11 pounds, about 7 percent of total body weight. It counts as an organ because it combines all four tissue types working together.
notes: The brain is a large organ protected by the skull, but it weighs far less than the skin. Students sometimes pick it because it is the most complex organ, which is a different idea from the largest.
Correct. The skin outweighs every other organ.
The lungs fill much of the thoracic cavity, but they are light because they are mostly air spaces. Choose them if the question asked which organs fill most of the thoracic cavity.
The liver is the largest internal organ and the heaviest gland, but it weighs much less than the skin. Pick it if the question asked for the largest organ inside the abdominal cavity.

questions.q: Which layer of the skin holds the blood vessels, nerves, and glands?
questions.why: The dermis is the connective tissue layer of the skin, and it contains blood vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles. Because the epidermis has no blood vessels of its own, it depends on diffusion from the dermis for nutrients. That is why the dermis is described as essential to the survival of the epidermis.
notes: The stratum granulosum is a middle epidermal stratum where keratinocytes start to die. Choose it if the question asked which stratum lies just deep to the corneum in thin skin.
The epidermis is avascular, meaning it has no blood vessels, and its glands only reach into it from below. Pick it if the question asked which skin layer is made of epithelium.

The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal stratum, the row of dividing cells on the basement membrane. It would be the answer for the layer that produces new keratinocytes, but like the rest of the epidermis it has no vessels.
Correct. The dermis contains the skin's vessels, nerves, and glands.

questions.q: A keratinocyte is born in the deepest stratum and is pushed toward the surface. Which stratum does it reach last?
questions.why: Keratinocytes are made in the stratum basale and are pushed upward as new cells form beneath them. As they rise they fill with keratin and die, and they end up in the stratum corneum at the surface, where they are eventually shed. This is true in both thick and thin skin, because the corneum is always the outermost stratum.
notes: The stratum granulosum is a middle stratum where cells begin to die. It would be the answer for the last stratum reached before the corneum in thin skin.
The stratum spinosum is the second stratum, directly above the basale, so the cell passes through it early. Pick it if the question asked which stratum the cell enters first after leaving the basale.
The stratum lucidum lies just deep to the corneum, and only in thick skin. Choose it if the question asked for the next-to-last stratum a cell passes through on the palm or sole.
Correct. The stratum corneum is the surface layer and the final stop before the cell is shed.

questions.q: Thick skin of the palms and soles has five epidermal strata. Which stratum is essentially missing in thin skin?
questions.why: Thin skin covers most of the body and has four strata: basale, spinosum, granulosum, and corneum. Thick skin of the palms, soles, and palmar surfaces of the digits adds a fifth, the stratum lucidum, a thin clear band between the granulosum and the corneum. These are the areas of greatest friction, which is why they carry the extra layer.
notes: The stratum corneum is present in all skin as the dead surface layer, although it is thicker in thick skin. It would be the answer if the question asked which stratum makes the biggest contribution to thick skin's thickness.
The stratum spinosum is present in all skin, directly above the basale. Choose it if the question asked which stratum lies just superficial to the basale.
Correct. The stratum lucidum is found in thick skin and is essentially absent in thin skin.
The stratum basale is present in all skin because it holds the dividing cells that renew the epidermis. Pick it if the question asked which stratum is deepest.

questions.q: Which epidermal cell contacts a sensory nerve ending to detect touch?
questions.why: Tactile cells, also called Merkel cells, are the least numerous epidermal cells and sit in the deepest layer of the epidermis. Each one contacts the flattened ending of a sensory neuron, called a tactile disc or Merkel disc. Together they detect light touch.
notes: Correct. Tactile (Merkel) cells pair with a sensory nerve ending to sense touch.
Keratinocytes make keratin and form most of the epidermis, but they are not touch receptors. Pick them if the question asked which cell makes up about 90 percent of the epidermis.
Intraepidermal macrophages (Langerhans cells) are immune cells that help recognize microbes entering the skin. Choose them if the question asked about immune defense in the epidermis.
Melanocytes make melanin, the pigment that shields DNA from UV light. They would be the answer for a question about skin color.

questions.q: Which dermal layer forms the dermal papillae, the finger-like projections that push up into the epidermis?
questions.why: The papillary layer is the superficial dermis, and its upper surface rises into small finger-shaped projections called dermal papillae. The papillae increase the contact area between dermis and epidermis, which helps anchor and feed the epidermis. On the palms, soles, and fingertips they are arranged in rows that raise the epidermal ridges we see as fingerprints.
notes: Correct. The papillary layer forms the dermal papillae.
The hypodermis lies beneath the skin and has no papillae. Choose it if the question asked which layer stores fat beneath the skin.
The reticular layer is the deep dermis with thick collagen bundles, and it does not form papillae. Pick it if the question asked which dermal layer holds the hair follicles and sweat glands.
The stratum granulosum is a middle layer of the epidermis, not the dermis. It would be the answer for the stratum where keratinocytes begin to die.

questions.q: Which dermal layer is made of dense irregular connective tissue and holds the hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands?
questions.why: The reticular layer is the deep four fifths of the dermis. It is dense irregular connective tissue, meaning thick collagen bundles running in many directions, which gives the skin its strength and resistance to stretching. It also holds the larger blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands.
notes: The hypodermis is the subcutaneous layer of adipose and areolar tissue below the skin. Choose it if the question asked where lamellated corpuscles and fat storage are found.
The stratum basale is epithelium, the deepest layer of the epidermis, not connective tissue. It would be the answer for where new keratinocytes are made.
Correct. The reticular layer is dense irregular connective tissue that houses the follicles and glands.
The papillary layer is the thin superficial dermis made of areolar connective tissue. Pick it if the question asked which layer contains the capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles.

questions.q: Which small muscle attaches to a hair follicle and pulls the hair upright, producing goose bumps?
questions.why: The arrector pili is a small band of smooth muscle that runs from the dermis to the side of a hair follicle. When it contracts, it pulls the hair shaft perpendicular to the skin surface and dimples the skin around it, producing goose bumps. Because it is smooth muscle, the contraction is involuntary.
notes: Correct. The arrector pili is the smooth muscle that stands the hair up.
The hair bulb is the onion-shaped base of the follicle where the hair grows. It would be the answer for the region that contains the hair matrix.
The hair root plexus is a network of sensory nerve endings wrapped around each follicle that detects light touch when the hair moves. Pick it if the question asked how a hair senses being brushed.
The dermal root sheath is the dermis that surrounds the follicle like a sleeve. Choose it if the question asked which connective tissue wraps the follicle.

questions.q: Which sweat gland is the most numerous and opens directly onto the skin surface?
questions.why: Eccrine sweat glands are found throughout most of the body, especially on the forehead, palms, and soles. Their coiled secretory part sits mostly in the deep dermis, and their duct runs up through the epidermis to open on the skin surface. They release watery sweat that cools the body as it evaporates.
notes: Sebaceous glands are oil glands, not sweat glands, and most open into hair follicles. They would be the answer for a question about sebum.

Apocrine sweat glands are found in the axillae, groin, and areolae, and their ducts open into hair follicles rather than onto the surface. Pick them if the question asked about sweat glands that empty into follicles.
Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands of the external ear canal that make earwax. Choose them if the question asked which glands open into the external auditory canal.
Correct. Eccrine glands are the most numerous sweat glands and open onto the skin surface.

questions.q: The cuticle of a nail is also known by what other name?
questions.why: The cuticle is the eponychium, a narrow band of epidermis that extends from the nail wall and adheres to the proximal margin of the nail. It is made of stratum corneum. The prefix epi means upon, which helps separate it from the hyponychium (hypo means below), the thickened layer beneath the free edge.
notes: The hyponychium is the thickened stratum corneum beneath the free edge that secures the nail to the fingertip. The look-alike name is the trap; choose it if the question asked about the tissue under the free edge.
The lunula is the whitish crescent at the proximal end of the nail body. Pick it if the question asked about the little moon shape on the nail.
The nail matrix is the epithelium proximal to the nail root where new nail cells are made. It would be the answer for the growth region of the nail.
Correct. The eponychium is the cuticle.

questions.q: Which gland secretes cerumen (earwax) into the external ear canal?
questions.why: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands found only in the external auditory canal. They secrete cerumen, a waxy material, onto the surface of the canal or into the ducts of nearby sebaceous glands. Cerumen helps trap dust and debris before it reaches the eardrum.
notes: Correct. Ceruminous glands produce cerumen in the external ear canal.
Mammary glands are also modified sweat glands, but they lie in the breasts and produce milk. Pick them if the question asked which modified sweat gland produces milk.
Sebaceous glands make oily sebum, and in the ear canal their ducts can receive cerumen, but they do not make it. Choose them if the question asked which glands secrete oil onto the hair.
Apocrine sweat glands release a thick sweat into hair follicles of the axillae and groin. They would be the answer for sweat glands that become active at puberty.

questions.q: Ceruminous glands and mammary glands are both described as modified versions of which gland type?
questions.why: Ceruminous glands of the ear canal and mammary glands of the breast are both modified sweat glands. Each keeps the basic plan of a sweat gland, a secretory portion with a duct, but makes a specialized product: cerumen in the ear and milk in the breast. Recognizing them as sweat gland relatives helps you group the skin glands into oil glands and sweat glands.
notes: Salivary glands are digestive glands around the mouth, not skin glands. They would be the answer for a question about glands that release saliva into the oral cavity.
Correct. Both ceruminous and mammary glands are modified sweat glands.
Sebaceous glands are the oil glands of the skin, a separate family from sweat glands. Pick them if the question asked which glands secrete sebum into hair follicles.
Tarsal glands are oil glands in the eyelids and are themselves a form of sebaceous gland. Choose them if the question asked which sebaceous glands lie along the eyelid margins.

questions.q: Which accessory structure of the skin is a plate of hard, dead keratinized cells covering the dorsal surface of the tip of a finger or toe?
questions.why: Nails are plates of tightly packed, hard, dead keratinized epidermal cells covering the dorsal surfaces of the distal parts of the digits. The nail body is comparable to the stratum corneum, except its cells hold a harder keratin and are not shed. Nails protect the fingertips and give counter pressure that helps us grasp and handle small objects.
notes: A hair is also made of dead keratinized cells, but it forms a thin strand rather than a flat plate. Pick it if the question asked which keratinized structure grows from a follicle.
A sebaceous gland is an oil gland that usually empties into a hair follicle. Choose it if the question asked which accessory structure secretes sebum.
A hair follicle is the sheath of epidermal and dermal tissue that surrounds the hair root. It would be the answer for the structure that holds a hair in the skin.
Correct. A nail is a flat plate of hard keratin on the dorsal fingertip or toe tip.

questions.q: Hair follicles, nails, and skin glands all develop from which layer of the skin, even though most of them reach down into the dermis?
questions.why: The accessory structures of the skin form as downgrowths of the epidermis. A hair follicle, for example, has an external root sheath that is a downward continuation of the epidermis, and the hair matrix arises from the stratum basale. Because follicles and glands are lined with epidermal cells living deep in the dermis, they can help regrow the epidermis after a partial-thickness burn.
notes: The papillary layer is the superficial dermis with capillary loops and touch receptors. Choose it if the question asked which layer forms the dermal papillae.

The hypodermis is the fatty layer beneath the skin, and some gland coils reach into it, but the structures do not form there. It would be the answer for where lamellated corpuscles and fat storage are found.
Correct. Hair, nails, and skin glands are epidermal in origin.
The dermis surrounds and supports follicles and glands, but it does not produce them. Pick it if the question asked which layer houses most of the follicles and glands.

questions.q: Besides the skin itself, which structures belong to the integumentary system?
options: The deep fascia and the periosteum
Superficial lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels
Hair, nails, skin glands, and sensory receptors
questions.why: The integumentary system is the skin (the cutaneous membrane) plus its associated structures: hair, oil glands, sweat glands, sensory receptors, and nails. These structures work with the skin to protect the body, regulate temperature, and sense the environment. Nearby tissues such as muscle, fascia, and lymph nodes belong to other systems.
notes: The deep fascia wraps muscles and the periosteum covers bones, so both lie deep to the skin. Choose them if the question asked what the hypodermis anchors the skin to.
Skeletal muscles and tendons belong to the muscular system and lie deep to the hypodermis. Pick them if the question asked which system moves the skeleton.
Superficial lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels lie beneath the skin, but they belong to the lymphatic system. They would be the answer for a question about structures that filter lymph.
Correct. Hair, nails, glands, and sensory receptors are the associated structures of the integumentary system.
questions.answerText: Hair, nails, skin glands, and sensory receptors

questions.q: What is the part of a hair that lies within the follicle, beneath the skin surface, called?
questions.why: A hair has two parts. The hair root is the portion that penetrates into the dermis, and sometimes the subcutaneous layer, inside the follicle. The hair shaft is the portion that projects above the skin surface, and both are made of dead keratinized cells.
notes: The hair follicle is the sheath of tissue that surrounds the root, not the hair itself. Choose it if the question asked which structure encloses the hair root.
The hair bulb is the onion-shaped base of the follicle that contains the dividing matrix. It would be the answer for the growth region at the bottom of the follicle.
The hair shaft is the part of the hair above the skin surface. Pick it if the question asked which part of the hair you can see or cut.
Correct. The hair root is the buried part of the hair within the follicle.

questions.q: What is the whitish crescent at the proximal end of the nail body called?
questions.why: The lunula, meaning little moon, is the crescent-shaped area at the proximal end of the nail body. It looks whitish because the epithelium beneath it is thickened, so the pink of the vascular tissue below does not show through. The rest of the nail body looks pink because blood vessels lie close beneath it.
notes: The hyponychium is thickened stratum corneum under the free edge that secures the nail to the fingertip. It would be the answer for the tissue under the tip of the nail.
The eponychium is the cuticle, the band of epidermis along the proximal nail wall. Pick it if the question asked for the other name of the cuticle.
Correct. The lunula is the pale crescent at the base of the nail body.
The free edge is the part of the nail extending past the fingertip, and it is white because no capillaries lie under it. Choose it if the question asked which part of the nail you trim.

questions.q: On the fingertips, dermal papillae push the epidermis up into epidermal ridges that form fingerprints. Besides forming fingerprints, what do these ridges do?
options: They anchor hairs that sense light touch
They secrete sweat that cools the hand
They increase grip and touch sensitivity
They store fat that cushions the fingertip
questions.why: Epidermal ridges increase the surface area where dermis meets epidermis, which raises the number of touch corpuscles and makes the fingertips more sensitive. The ridges also increase friction, which improves grip. They form only where dermal papillae are well developed and lined up in rows, as on the palms, soles, and fingertips.
notes: The fingertips are thick skin and have no hair follicles. Hair root plexuses would be the answer for how hairy skin senses light touch, but they do not exist on the palms or fingertips.
Sweat is made by eccrine sweat glands, which open along the ridges but are separate structures. Pick sweat glands if the question asked what keeps the palms moist or cools the body.
Correct. The ridges improve grip by adding friction and improve touch by adding receptors.
Fat storage is the job of the hypodermis, the adipose layer beneath the skin. It would be the answer if the question asked which layer cushions and insulates.
questions.answerText: They increase grip and touch sensitivity

questions.q: Looking at a slide of the epidermis, you see a single row of cube-shaped, actively dividing cells resting on the basement membrane. Which stratum is this?
questions.why: The stratum basale is a single row of cells sitting on the basement membrane, the thin layer that separates the epidermis from the dermis. These cells divide to make new keratinocytes, and the layer also holds melanocytes and tactile cells. On a slide, look for the one-cell-thick row right at the border with the dermis.
notes: The stratum spinosum is several layers thick and sits just above the basale, with cells that look spiny on slides. Choose it if the slide showed multiple rows of spiny cells above the basal row.
The stratum corneum is many layers of flat, dead cells at the surface. It would be the answer if the slide showed the pale, flaky top of the epidermis.

The stratum granulosum shows several rows of flattening cells filled with dark granules, in the middle of the epidermis. Pick it if the slide showed cells with dark granules just beneath the clear or dead layers.
Correct. A single dividing row on the basement membrane is the stratum basale.

questions.q: A skin section from the sole of the foot shows a thin, clear band just deep to the surface layer. Which stratum is this, and what does it tell you about the sample?
options: The stratum lucidum, so the sample is thick skin
The stratum basale, so the sample is thin skin
The stratum granulosum, so the sample is thin skin
The stratum spinosum, so the sample is thick skin
questions.why: The stratum lucidum is a thin, clear band between the granulosum and the corneum, and it is present only in thick skin. Thick skin covers the palms, soles, and palmar surfaces of the digits, the areas of greatest friction. Finding a lucidum on a slide is the quickest way to label the sample as thick skin.
notes: Correct. A clear band under the corneum is the stratum lucidum, which marks thick skin.
The stratum basale is the single row of dividing cells at the bottom of the epidermis, not just under the surface. It would be the answer for the deepest stratum in any skin.

The stratum granulosum lies deep to the lucidum and shows dark granules rather than a clear band, and it is present in both skin types. Pick it if the band were granular and sat directly under the corneum in thin skin.
The stratum spinosum is the spiny layer above the basale, present in both skin types and not clear. Choose it if the question asked which stratum sits directly superficial to the basale.
questions.answerText: The stratum lucidum, so the sample is thick skin

questions.q: An intradermal injection, such as a tuberculosis skin test, places a small amount of fluid in which layer?
options: The skeletal muscle beneath the hypodermis
questions.why: Intradermal means within the dermis, so the needle tip sits just under the epidermis but above the hypodermis. Fluid placed there raises a small bump on the skin surface. The word itself tells you the layer: intra means within.
notes: Correct. An intradermal injection places fluid within the dermis.
Skeletal muscle lies deep to the hypodermis and is the target of an intramuscular injection. Choose it if the question asked where an intramuscular vaccine is delivered.
The stratum corneum is the dead surface layer of the epidermis, too thin and too superficial to hold an injection. Pick it if the question asked which layer a topical cream first contacts.
The hypodermis is the fatty subcutaneous layer, the target of a subcutaneous injection such as insulin. It would be the answer if the question named a subcutaneous route.

questions.q: A partial-thickness burn destroys the epidermis over an area but leaves the deeper dermis with its hair follicles and sweat glands intact. Where will new epidermal cells come from?
options: From fibroblasts in the reticular layer of the dermis
From adipocytes in the fatty hypodermis below
From dead keratinized cells of the stratum corneum
From epidermal cells lining surviving follicles and glands
questions.why: Hair follicles and sweat glands are lined with epidermal cells that extend deep into the dermis. When a burn destroys the surface epidermis but spares the deeper dermis, these surviving epidermal cells divide and spread out to rebuild the epidermis. That is why a partial-thickness burn can heal without a graft, while a full-thickness burn that destroys the follicles and glands usually cannot.
notes: Fibroblasts are connective tissue cells that make collagen and help form scar tissue, but they cannot make epidermis. Pick them if the question asked which cells build the fibers of the dermis.
Adipocytes are fat cells of the hypodermis and do not form epithelium. They would be the answer if the question asked which cells store fat beneath the skin.

Cells of the stratum corneum are dead and cannot divide, and in this burn they are gone anyway. Students pick them because they are epidermal, but only living, dividing epidermal cells can rebuild the layer.
Correct. The epidermal linings of surviving follicles and glands regrow the surface epidermis.
questions.answerText: From epidermal cells lining surviving follicles and glands

questions.q: A section of axillary skin shows sweat glands whose ducts open into hair follicles rather than onto the skin surface. Which gland type is this?
questions.why: Apocrine sweat glands are found in the skin of the axillae, groin, areolae, and bearded regions of the face, and their ducts open into hair follicles. Their sweat contains the same components as eccrine sweat plus lipids and proteins. Eccrine glands, by contrast, open directly onto the skin surface.
notes: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands found only in the external ear canal. They would be the answer if the section came from the ear canal.
Eccrine sweat glands are the most numerous sweat glands and open directly onto the skin surface. Pick them if the ducts opened through pores on the skin.
Correct. Apocrine sweat glands empty into hair follicles in the axillae and groin.
Sebaceous glands also open into hair follicles, but they are oil glands that secrete sebum, not sweat. Choose them if the glands were described as producing oil.

questions.q: A skin specimen lacks a stratum lucidum, has a thin stratum corneum, and contains many hair follicles. From which site was it most likely taken?
questions.why: Skin with no stratum lucidum, a thin corneum, and hair follicles is thin skin, which covers every part of the body except the palms, soles, and palmar surfaces of the digits. The posterior forearm is ordinary hairy skin, so it fits. Thick skin has a lucidum and a thick corneum but no hair follicles.
notes: Correct. The posterior forearm is hairy thin skin without a lucidum.
The sole of the foot is thick skin, with the thickest corneum in the body and no hair. It would be the answer for a specimen with a very thick corneum and a clear lucidum.
The palm is thick skin with a stratum lucidum and no hair follicles. Pick it if the specimen had five strata and no hair.
The fingertip pad is thick skin with epidermal ridges and no hair follicles. Choose it if the specimen showed fingerprint ridges and a lucidum.

questions.q: A specimen shows a plate of hard keratin over the dorsal tip of a finger, with dividing cells hidden under the skin fold at its proximal end. Which pair names the structure and its growth region?
options: The nail and the nail matrix
The hair and the hair bulb
questions.why: A plate of hard keratin over the dorsal fingertip is a nail. Its growth region is the nail matrix, epithelium proximal to the nail root, tucked under the skin fold, where dividing cells produce new nail. The new cells push the nail body forward toward the free edge.
notes: The hyponychium is thickened stratum corneum under the free edge at the distal end of the nail. Choose it if the question asked what secures the nail to the fingertip.

The lunula is the pale crescent at the proximal end of the visible nail body, not the hidden region of dividing cells. It would be the answer if the question asked about the whitish half-moon you can see.
Correct. The structure is the nail and its growth region is the nail matrix.
A hair is a strand, not a plate, and its growth region is the hair bulb at the base of a follicle. Pick this pair if the specimen showed a strand growing from a follicle.
questions.answerText: The nail and the nail matrix

questions.q: A needle is pushed from the skin surface straight down to a muscle. In what order does it pass through the layers?
questions.why: From the surface inward, the needle crosses the epidermis, then the dermis, then the hypodermis, and finally reaches the muscle beneath the deep fascia. The epidermis and dermis make up the skin, and the hypodermis is the fatty layer that anchors the skin to the muscle. This same order explains injection routes: intradermal stops in the dermis, subcutaneous in the hypodermis, and intramuscular in the muscle.
notes: This order puts the dermis on top, but the epidermis is always the surface layer. Students make this mix-up when they forget that the epidermis lies on top of the dermis, not beneath it.

This order places the hypodermis between the two skin layers, but the epidermis and dermis are directly attached to each other. Students choose it when they confuse the hypodermis with a layer inside the skin.

This order starts with the hypodermis, which is the deepest of the three layers. It would only make sense if the needle were traveling from the muscle outward, and even then the epidermis would come last.
Correct. Epidermis, dermis, hypodermis, then muscle is the surface-to-deep order.

questions.q: In thick skin, in what order does a keratinocyte pass through the strata, from where it is born to the surface?
questions.why: A keratinocyte is born in the stratum basale, then moves through the spinosum, the granulosum, the lucidum, and finally the corneum, where it is shed. The mnemonic Baby Screams Grandpa Loves Coffee gives this deep-to-superficial order. In thin skin the sequence is the same except that the lucidum is missing.
notes: This order swaps the spinosum and granulosum. The spinosum sits directly on the basale, and the granulosum comes after it, so this is a common swap of the two middle layers.
This is the correct list run backward, from surface to deep. It would be the answer if the question asked for the strata from superficial to deep.
Correct. Basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum is the deep-to-surface path.

This order starts in the spinosum and ends in the lucidum, but cells are born in the basale and the corneum is always the surface. Students choose it when they lose track of which layers sit at the two ends.

questions.q: Moving from above the skin surface down to the base of a follicle, which order names the hair regions correctly?
options: Hair bulb, hair root, hair shaft
Hair root, hair shaft, hair bulb
Hair shaft, hair root, hair bulb
Hair shaft, hair bulb, hair root
questions.why: The hair shaft projects above the skin, the hair root is the part buried in the dermis inside the follicle, and the hair bulb is the onion-shaped base at the bottom of the follicle. The bulb holds the dividing matrix that grows the hair. So moving downward you meet shaft, then root, then bulb.
notes: This is the correct order run backward, from the base up to the surface. It would be the answer if the question asked for the regions from deep to superficial.
This order puts the root above the shaft, but the shaft is the only part above the skin. Students choose it when they mix up which term means the visible part.
Correct. Shaft, root, bulb is the order from the surface down.
This order puts the bulb above the root, but the bulb is the very bottom of the follicle. It confuses the growing base with the buried middle part of the hair.
questions.answerText: Hair shaft, hair root, hair bulb

questions.q: A section through the thick skin of the palm runs from the outermost epidermal stratum down to the dermal layer that holds the sweat glands. Which pair names the first stratum and the last dermal layer reached?
options: Stratum lucidum first, then the papillary layer
Stratum corneum first, then the reticular layer
Stratum basale first, then the papillary layer
Stratum corneum first, then the papillary layer
questions.why: The outermost stratum in all skin is the stratum corneum, even in thick skin where the lucidum lies just beneath it. The sweat glands sit in the reticular layer, the deep dense irregular part of the dermis. The papillary layer above it holds capillary loops and touch receptors, not the gland coils.
notes: The stratum lucidum lies just beneath the corneum in thick skin, so it is reached second. Pick the lucidum if the question asked which stratum appears directly under the surface layer of the palm.
Correct. The section starts in the stratum corneum and ends in the reticular layer.

The stratum basale is the deepest stratum, so it cannot be the first one reached from the surface. This pair would describe the last epidermal layer and the first dermal layer a section passes through.

The corneum is correct as the first layer, but the papillary layer holds capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles, not sweat glands. Choose the papillary layer if the question asked where the dermal papillae are.
questions.answerText: Stratum corneum first, then the reticular layer

questions.q: Which order lists the superficial skin layer, the superficial dermal layer, and the deep dermal layer, from superficial to deep?
questions.why: The epidermis is the surface layer of the skin. Beneath it, the dermis has a thin superficial papillary layer of areolar connective tissue and a thick deep reticular layer of dense irregular connective tissue. The papilla in papillary refers to the dermal papillae that push up into the epidermis, a reminder that this layer touches the epidermis.
notes: This order starts with the dermis, but the dermis is the deep skin layer and the papillary and reticular layers are parts of it. Students choose it when they forget that the epidermis sits above everything else.
This order skips the papillary layer and adds the hypodermis, which is below the skin. It would fit a question asking for the epidermis, the deep dermis, and the layer under the skin.
Correct. Epidermis, papillary layer, reticular layer runs from superficial to deep.
This order reverses the two dermal layers. The papillary layer forms the papillae that touch the epidermis, so it must come before the reticular layer.

questions.q: Two skin samples are compared. The first has five epidermal strata and no hair follicles. The second has four strata and many hair follicles. Which statement is correct?
options: The second sample is thick skin, and it lacks the stratum spinosum
The first sample is thin skin, and the second lacks the stratum corneum
The first sample is thick skin, and the second lacks the stratum lucidum
The second sample is thick skin, and it lacks the stratum basale
questions.why: Thick skin has all five strata and no hair follicles, so the first sample is thick skin. Thin skin has four strata because it essentially lacks the stratum lucidum, and it carries hair follicles, so the second sample is thin skin. The basale, spinosum, granulosum, and corneum are present in both kinds of skin.
notes: The second sample is thin skin, and the spinosum is present in both skin types. Pick the spinosum only if the question asked which stratum lies directly above the basale.
Five strata means thick skin, not thin, and every skin type has a stratum corneum at the surface. This option would only fit if thin skin were defined by a missing surface layer, which it is not.
Correct. Five strata with no hair is thick skin, and the four-strata sample lacks the lucidum.
The second sample has hair, which marks thin skin, and no skin lacks the stratum basale because it is the dividing layer. Students choose this when they link more hair with thicker skin.
questions.answerText: The first sample is thick skin, and the second lacks the stratum lucidum

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the blood supply of the epidermis and the dermis?
options: Neither layer has vessels, so both are fed from the hypodermis
The dermis has no blood vessels, and the epidermis holds the vessels and nerves
Both layers have their own capillary beds of equal size
The epidermis has no blood vessels, and the dermis holds the vessels, nerves, and glands
questions.why: The epidermis is avascular, meaning it has no blood vessels, so its living cells are fed by diffusion from capillaries in the dermis. The dermis is a vascular connective tissue that holds blood vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles. This is why the dermis is essential to the survival of the epidermis.
notes: The dermis has its own extensive vessel network, including capillary loops in the dermal papillae. The hypodermis does carry large vessels, but it is not the direct supply for the epidermis.
This statement reverses the two layers. The dermis is the vascular layer, and the epidermis is the one without vessels.
Only the dermis has capillary beds; the epidermis has none. Students choose this when they assume every living layer must have its own blood supply.
Correct. The epidermis is avascular and depends on the vascular dermis.
questions.answerText: The epidermis has no blood vessels, and the dermis holds the vessels, nerves, and glands

questions.q: Which list names the four skin glands compared in this course?
options: Sebaceous, eccrine sweat, apocrine sweat, and ceruminous glands
Eccrine sweat, apocrine sweat, ceruminous, and salivary glands
Sebaceous, apocrine sweat, ceruminous, and gastric glands
Sebaceous, eccrine sweat, apocrine sweat, and lacrimal glands
questions.why: The four skin glands are the sebaceous (oil) glands, the eccrine sweat glands, the apocrine sweat glands, and the ceruminous glands of the ear canal. They differ in where they are found, where their ducts open, what they secrete, and when they become active. All four develop from the epidermis and sit in the dermis or the upper subcutaneous layer.
notes: Correct. Sebaceous, eccrine, apocrine, and ceruminous are the four skin glands.
Salivary glands are digestive glands that release saliva into the mouth, not skin glands. They would be the answer for a question about the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands.
Gastric glands lie in the stomach lining and secrete gastric juice, so they belong to the digestive system. Choose them if the question asked which glands are found in the stomach mucosa.
Lacrimal glands make tears and sit in the orbit above the eye, so they are not skin glands. Pick them if the question asked which gland produces tears.
questions.answerText: Sebaceous, eccrine sweat, apocrine sweat, and ceruminous glands

questions.q: Which statement about the hypodermis is correct?
options: It lies deep to the dermis, outside the skin
It is another name for the reticular layer
It is the deepest layer of the skin proper
It lies between the epidermis and the dermis
questions.why: The hypodermis, or subcutaneous layer, lies beneath the dermis and is not part of the skin. It is made of areolar and adipose tissue that stores fat and anchors the skin to the fascia around muscles and bones. The skin proper ends at the bottom of the reticular layer of the dermis.
notes: Correct. The hypodermis is beneath the dermis and outside the skin proper.
The reticular layer is the deep layer of the dermis, made of dense irregular connective tissue. Pick it if the question asked for the deep part of the dermis, not the fatty layer beneath the skin.
The deepest layer of the skin proper is the dermis, specifically its reticular layer. Students choose this when they count the hypodermis as part of the skin.
Nothing lies between the epidermis and dermis except the basement membrane. This option confuses the hypodermis with the boundary between the two skin layers.
questions.answerText: It lies deep to the dermis, outside the skin

questions.q: Which pressure receptor sits deep in the skin, in the hypodermis with the large blood vessels?
questions.why: Lamellated corpuscles are large, onion-like nerve endings sensitive to pressure, and they sit deep, in the hypodermis with the large blood vessels. Because they are deep, they respond to firm pressure and vibration rather than light touch. The light touch receptors sit closer to the surface, in the dermal papillae and the epidermis.
notes: Meissner corpuscles are touch receptors in the dermal papillae of the papillary layer. Pick them if the question asked which receptor sits in the dermal papillae for fine touch.
Tactile (Merkel) discs are nerve endings in contact with tactile cells in the deepest layer of the epidermis. They would be the answer for the touch receptor found in the epidermis.
The hair root plexus is a network of nerve endings around each hair follicle in the dermis. Choose it if the question asked how a hair senses being moved.
Correct. The lamellated corpuscle is the deep pressure receptor of the hypodermis.

questions.q: Which stratum lies directly superficial to the stratum basale?
questions.why: The stratum spinosum is the second stratum from the bottom, resting directly on the stratum basale. It is several cells thick, and its cells look spiny on slides. Using the mnemonic Baby Screams Grandpa Loves Coffee, the S for spinosum comes right after the B for basale.
notes: The stratum corneum is the surface stratum, the farthest from the basale. Choose it if the question asked which stratum forms the outer surface.
The stratum granulosum is the third stratum, above the spinosum. Pick it if the question asked which stratum lies directly superficial to the spinosum.
Correct. The stratum spinosum sits directly on the basale.
The stratum lucidum is the fourth stratum, present only in thick skin. It would be the answer for the stratum directly deep to the corneum on the palm or sole.

questions.q: In thin skin, which stratum lies directly beneath the stratum corneum?
questions.why: Thin skin has four strata: basale, spinosum, granulosum, and corneum. Because the stratum lucidum is essentially missing in thin skin, the granulosum lies directly beneath the corneum. In thick skin the lucidum would slip in between those two layers.
notes: Correct. Without a lucidum, the granulosum sits right under the corneum.
The stratum basale is the deepest stratum, far from the corneum. Choose it if the question asked which stratum rests on the basement membrane.
The stratum lucidum lies directly beneath the corneum only in thick skin, and thin skin essentially lacks it. Pick it if the question asked the same thing about the palm or sole.
The stratum spinosum is the second layer from the bottom, beneath the granulosum. It would be the answer for the stratum directly above the basale.

questions.q: Where in the body would you find skin that has a stratum lucidum?
questions.why: The stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin, which covers the palms, the soles, and the palmar surfaces of the digits. These are the areas of greatest friction and pressure. Everywhere else, including hairy areas such as the scalp, is thin skin without a lucidum.
notes: The scalp is thin skin with many hair follicles, and thick skin never has hair. Pick the scalp if the question asked where terminal hairs are densest.
The upper back is thin skin, even though its dermis is quite thick. Students pick it because they confuse a thick dermis with thick skin, which is defined by the epidermis.
The eyelids are among the thinnest skin of the body and have no lucidum. Choose the eyelids if the question asked where tarsal glands, a form of sebaceous gland, are found.
Correct. The palms and soles are thick skin with a stratum lucidum.

questions.q: Besides keratin, keratinocytes produce lamellar granules. What do these granules release?
questions.why: Lamellar granules are made by keratinocytes and release a water-repellent sealant between the cells of the upper epidermis. The sealant decreases water entry and loss and helps block foreign material. Together with keratin, it makes the epidermis a protective barrier.
notes: Watery sweat is made by eccrine sweat glands and released through pores. Choose it if the question asked what eccrine glands release to cool the body.
Correct. Lamellar granules release a water-repellent sealant.
Sebum is made by sebaceous glands in the dermis and released into hair follicles. It would be the answer if the question asked what oil glands secrete.
Melanin is made by melanocytes and passed to keratinocytes, not made by keratinocytes. Pick melanin if the question asked what melanocytes transfer to keratinocytes.

questions.q: Skin color differs between people mainly because of which difference?
options: The number of melanocytes in the epidermis
The number of blood vessels in the dermis
The amount of melanin the melanocytes make
The thickness of the stratum corneum
questions.why: The number of melanocytes is about the same in all people. Differences in skin color come from how much pigment those melanocytes produce and transfer to keratinocytes. Exposure to UV light raises melanin production, which is what a tan is.
notes: The number of melanocytes is about the same in everyone, so it does not explain color differences. Students choose this when they assume darker skin must have more pigment cells. Melanocyte number would be the answer for vitiligo, where patches of skin lose their melanocytes.

Dermal blood vessels add a pink to red tone through hemoglobin, and their content changes with flushing or low oxygen. They would be the answer for color changes like erythema or cyanosis, not for differences between people.
Correct. Color depends on how much melanin the melanocytes make and pass on.
Corneum thickness changes with friction, which is why the palms and soles are thick skin, but it is not what sets a person's skin color. Pick it if the question asked why thick skin is thick.
questions.answerText: The amount of melanin the melanocytes make

questions.q: Which tissue makes up the papillary layer of the dermis?
questions.why: The papillary layer is the thin, superficial dermis, made of areolar connective tissue with thin collagen and fine elastic fibers. This loose tissue leaves room for capillary loops, Meissner corpuscles, and free nerve endings in the dermal papillae. The deeper reticular layer is the tougher dense irregular connective tissue.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue has parallel collagen fibers and forms tendons and ligaments, not the dermis. Choose it if the question asked what tissue connects muscle to bone.
Dense irregular connective tissue makes up the reticular layer, the deep four fifths of the dermis. Pick it if the question asked about the deep dermal layer.
Adipose tissue makes up most of the hypodermis beneath the skin. It would be the answer for the subcutaneous layer.
Correct. The papillary layer is areolar connective tissue.

questions.q: Which dermal layer gives the skin most of its strength and its resistance to stretching?
questions.why: The reticular layer makes up about four fifths of the dermis and is built of thick bundles of collagen in a net-like arrangement. That collagen gives the skin its strength, while its elastic fibers allow stretch and recoil. When this layer is overstretched and torn, as in pregnancy, the result is visible stretch marks.
notes: The hypodermis is the fatty layer beneath the skin, made for fat storage and anchoring. Choose it if the question asked which layer insulates and cushions.
Correct. The reticular layer's thick collagen bundles provide strength.
The stratum spinosum is an epidermal stratum, not part of the dermis. It would be the answer for the stratum directly above the basale.

The papillary layer is the thin superficial dermis with fine fibers, built to anchor and feed the epidermis rather than to resist pulling. Pick it if the question asked which layer forms the dermal papillae.

questions.q: Which type of tissue makes up the arrector pili?
questions.why: The arrector pili is a small band of smooth muscle that connects the dermis to a hair follicle. Smooth muscle contracts involuntarily, which is why goose bumps appear on their own when you are cold or frightened. When it contracts, it pulls the hair shaft perpendicular to the skin surface.
notes: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, which cannot contract. Choose it if the question asked what attaches a skeletal muscle to bone.
Correct. The arrector pili is smooth muscle, so it contracts involuntarily.
Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart wall. It would be the answer for the muscle tissue with intercalated discs.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary, striated muscle attached to bones, such as the muscles of facial expression. Pick it if the question asked which muscle tissue moves the skin of the face.

questions.q: Where does the duct of most sebaceous glands empty?
options: Directly onto the skin surface through a pore
Into the blood vessels of the dermis
questions.why: Most sebaceous glands are connected to a hair follicle, so the sebum coats the hair and then spreads onto the skin. This is why sebaceous glands are absent from the palms and soles, which have no hair follicles. A few, such as those on the lips, open directly onto the surface.
notes: Opening directly onto the surface through a pore describes eccrine sweat glands. Pick it if the question asked where the ducts of the most numerous sweat glands open.
Releasing a product into the blood describes endocrine glands, which have no ducts. Sebaceous glands are exocrine, so choose this only for a question about hormone-secreting glands.
The external ear canal receives cerumen from ceruminous glands. It would be the answer if the question asked where ceruminous glands release their product.
Correct. Most sebaceous ducts open into a hair follicle.

questions.q: Where is the coiled secretory portion of most eccrine sweat glands, and where does the duct open?
options: In the subcutaneous layer, with the duct opening into the ear canal
In the deep dermis, with the duct opening into a hair follicle
In the stratum basale, with the duct opening onto the skin surface
In the deep dermis, with the duct opening onto the skin surface
questions.why: The coiled secretory part of an eccrine sweat gland lies mostly in the deep dermis, sometimes reaching the upper subcutaneous layer. Its duct winds up through the dermis and epidermis to open as a pore on the skin surface. That direct route lets sweat spread over the skin and cool the body as it evaporates.
notes: A secretory portion in the subcutaneous layer with output into the ear canal describes ceruminous glands. Choose it if the question asked where earwax is made.
Opening into a hair follicle describes apocrine sweat glands and sebaceous glands. Pick this if the question asked about the sweat glands of the axillae and groin.
The stratum basale is an epidermal layer and cannot hold a gland's secretory coil. Students choose this because the duct does pass through the epidermis, but the gland itself sits in the dermis.
Correct. Eccrine glands coil in the deep dermis and open onto the surface.
questions.answerText: In the deep dermis, with the duct opening onto the skin surface

questions.q: A hair has three concentric layers. Which layer forms the major part of the hair shaft?
questions.why: Both the hair root and shaft have three layers. The medulla is the inner core of 2 to 3 rows of cells, the cortex is the thick middle layer of elongated cells that forms most of the shaft, and the cuticle is a single outer layer of thin, flat, heavily keratinized cells. Melanin passes into the cortex and medulla, so the cortex carries much of the hair's color.
notes: The hair cuticle is the single outermost layer of flat keratinized cells, not to be confused with the nail cuticle. It would be the answer for the outermost layer of the hair.
Correct. The cortex makes up most of the hair shaft.
The medulla is the inner core of the hair, only 2 to 3 rows of cells. Pick it if the question asked for the innermost layer.
The hair matrix is the layer of dividing cells in the hair bulb that grows the hair, not a layer of the shaft. Choose it if the question asked where hair cells are made.

questions.q: In thin skin, which order lists the strata a keratinocyte passes through, from where it is born to the surface?
questions.why: Thin skin has four strata. A keratinocyte is born in the stratum basale, then moves through the spinosum and granulosum, and ends in the corneum at the surface. Thin skin essentially lacks the stratum lucidum, so that step is skipped.
notes: This order swaps the spinosum and granulosum. The spinosum sits directly on the basale, so this is a mix-up of the two middle layers.
This five-strata order is correct for thick skin, which has a stratum lucidum. Pick it if the question asked about the palm or sole.
This is the thin skin order run backward, from surface to deep. It would be the answer if the question asked for the strata from superficial to deep.
Correct. Basale, spinosum, granulosum, corneum is the thin skin path.

questions.q: The epidermal ridges of the palms and soles, the basis of fingerprints, are raised by which structures?
options: Dead cells of the stratum corneum
Collagen bundles of the reticular layer
Dermal papillae of the papillary layer
questions.why: Dermal papillae are finger-shaped projections of the papillary layer that push up into the underside of the epidermis. In thick skin they are well developed and lined up in parallel rows, so the epidermis above them forms ridges. Those ridges are the fingerprints, and their pattern is set by the dermis beneath.
notes: The adipose lobules of the hypodermis cushion and insulate, well below the skin. They would be the answer for the layer that stores fat.
The stratum corneum follows the ridges at the surface, but it does not create them. Choose it if the question asked which layer forms the visible surface of a fingerprint.
The reticular layer's collagen bundles give the skin strength but lie too deep to shape the epidermis. Pick them if the question asked which dermal structure resists stretching.
Correct. Rows of dermal papillae push the epidermis up into ridges.
questions.answerText: Dermal papillae of the papillary layer

questions.q: A nurse must place an injection in the hypodermis. Which injection route reaches that layer?
questions.why: Subcutaneous means beneath the skin, and the hypodermis is the subcutaneous layer, so a subcutaneous injection places medication in the fatty tissue under the dermis. Insulin is a common example. The route names follow the layers from shallow to deep: intradermal, subcutaneous, then intramuscular.
notes: An intradermal injection stops in the dermis, above the hypodermis. Pick it if the question asked how a tuberculosis skin test is given.
An intravenous injection goes directly into a vein, into the blood rather than a tissue layer. Choose it if the question asked how medication is delivered straight into the bloodstream.
An intramuscular injection passes through the hypodermis into skeletal muscle. It would be the answer for a vaccine given into the deltoid.
Correct. A subcutaneous injection targets the hypodermis.

questions.q: In which stratum of the epidermis are tactile (Merkel) cells located?
questions.why: Tactile (Merkel) cells are the least numerous epidermal cells and sit in the deepest layer of the epidermis, the stratum basale. That position puts them right above the dermis, where each one can contact the flattened ending of a sensory neuron, the tactile disc. Together they detect light touch.
notes: The stratum granulosum is a middle layer where keratinocytes begin to die. It would be the answer for the stratum just beneath the corneum in thin skin.
The stratum spinosum is the layer just above the basale, several cells thick. Pick it if the question asked which stratum lies directly superficial to the basale.
The stratum corneum is dead surface cells, which cannot serve as living sensory cells. Choose it if the question asked which stratum is constantly shed.
Correct. Tactile cells sit in the stratum basale, the deepest stratum.

questions.q: Capillary loops, Meissner corpuscles, and free nerve endings are found together in which structures?
questions.why: The dermal papillae of the papillary layer hold three things you identify in lab: capillary loops that feed the epidermis by diffusion, Meissner corpuscles for touch and pressure, and free nerve endings for temperature, light touch, and itching. Their position right beneath the epidermis is what makes them suited to these jobs. Being close to the surface lets the receptors sense fine touch and lets the capillaries supply the avascular epidermis.
notes: Correct. The dermal papillae hold capillary loops, Meissner corpuscles, and free nerve endings.
The hypodermis holds lamellated corpuscles and large blood vessels, not capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles. Choose it if the question asked where deep pressure receptors lie.
The hair bulb holds the hair matrix and surrounds the papilla of the hair, a separate knob of vessels that feeds the growing hair. Pick it if the question asked where hair cells divide.
The epidermis is avascular and holds no capillary loops or Meissner corpuscles, though it does contain tactile discs. It would be the answer if the question asked where tactile (Merkel) cells sit.

questions.q: Which feature is present in thin skin but absent from thick skin?
questions.why: Thin skin covers most of the body and carries hair follicles, arrector pili muscles, and sebaceous glands. Thick skin, on the palms, soles, and palmar surfaces of the digits, has none of these. Thick skin instead adds a stratum lucidum, epidermal ridges, and a greater number of sweat glands.
notes: Correct. Hair follicles are found in thin skin and absent from thick skin.
Eccrine sweat glands are present in both skin types, and they are more numerous in thick skin. Choose them if the question asked which glands are most concentrated on the palms.
The stratum lucidum is the opposite case: present in thick skin and essentially lacking in thin skin. Pick it if the question asked which feature thick skin has that thin skin lacks.
Epidermal ridges form in thick skin, where dermal papillae are well developed and in rows. They would be the answer for a feature found on the fingertips but not the forearm.

questions.q: At what stage of life do apocrine sweat glands become active?
questions.why: Apocrine sweat glands, found in the axillae, groin, and areolae, begin secreting at puberty. Their sweat contains lipids and proteins in addition to the usual components, and it empties into hair follicles. Sebaceous glands also become much more active at puberty, which is part of why body odor and acne often start in the teen years.
notes: Early childhood is a quiet period for these glands; sebaceous glands, for example, stay relatively inactive through childhood. Students choose it when they guess that glands switch on gradually as a child grows.
Older adulthood is not when any skin gland turns on; gland activity generally declines with age. This choice reflects a guess rather than a real onset time.
Soon after birth is when eccrine sweat glands and ceruminous glands begin to work. Pick it if the question asked about the onset of eccrine sweating.
Correct. Apocrine sweat glands become active at puberty.

questions.q: A shallow paper cut stays entirely within the epidermis. What would you expect to happen?
options: It does not bleed, because the epidermis has no blood vessels
It bleeds slowly, because the stratum lucidum holds small veins
It bleeds, because arteries run through the stratum basale
It bleeds heavily, because capillary loops lie in the stratum corneum
questions.why: The epidermis is avascular, meaning it has no blood vessels of its own. A cut that stays within it does not reach any vessels, so it does not bleed. Bleeding begins only when a cut reaches the dermis, where the capillary loops of the dermal papillae and deeper vessels are found.
notes: Correct. The epidermis is avascular, so a cut confined to it does not bleed.
The stratum lucidum is a clear layer of dead cells found only in thick skin, with no veins. It would be the answer if the question asked which stratum appears only on the palms and soles.
The stratum basale is a row of dividing epithelial cells with no arteries. Students choose this because the basale is the deepest stratum, closest to the dermis, but the vessels stop at the dermis.
Capillary loops are in the dermal papillae of the papillary dermis, not in the stratum corneum. Pick capillary loops if the question asked which vessels supply the epidermis by diffusion.
questions.answerText: It does not bleed, because the epidermis has no blood vessels

questions.q: A burn blisters and reaches into the dermis but does not destroy its full thickness. How is this burn classified?
questions.why: Burn classes follow the skin layers. A partial-thickness burn reaches into the dermis and blisters because the junction between dermis and epidermis fails. It can still heal on its own because surviving hair follicles and sweat glands, lined with epidermal cells, lie deep in the dermis.
notes: Correct. A blistering burn into, but not through, the dermis is partial thickness.
A fourth-degree burn extends beyond the skin into deeper tissues such as muscle or bone. Choose it only if the burn reached structures below the hypodermis.
A full-thickness burn destroys the entire dermis and its follicles and glands, so it usually needs a graft. It would be the answer if the burn went all the way through the dermis.
A superficial burn involves the epidermis only, like a mild sunburn, and heals because the stratum basale is intact. Pick it if the burn were red and painful without blisters.

questions.q: A full-thickness burn destroys the epidermis and dermis, and the center of the burn is often painless. Why?
options: The skin regrows too quickly for pain to register
The hypodermis blocks pain signals from the dermis
The epidermis never had any sensory endings
The nerve endings in the dermis have been destroyed
questions.why: Most of the skin's sensory receptors, including free nerve endings that detect pain and temperature, lie in the dermis. A full-thickness burn destroys the dermis, so those receptors are destroyed too, and the center of the burn may feel numb. The less damaged edges, where nerve endings survive, are usually very painful.
notes: A full-thickness burn cannot regrow on its own because the stratum basale and the follicles and glands are gone. Students choose this when they mix up how fast skin heals with whether it can sense pain.
The hypodermis does not block pain signals; it holds fat, large vessels, and lamellated corpuscles. It would be the answer if the question asked where deep pressure receptors are found.

The epidermis does contain sensory structures, such as tactile discs, and nerve endings reach it from the dermis. This choice reflects the true fact that the epidermis has no blood vessels, which students confuse with having no nerves.
Correct. The burn destroys the dermal nerve endings that would sense pain.
questions.answerText: The nerve endings in the dermis have been destroyed

questions.q: A superficial burn damages the epidermis but spares the stratum basale, and the skin repairs itself without a graft. Why does sparing this layer allow healing?
options: It holds the dividing cells that rebuild the epidermis
It stores the skin's water supply
It forms the dead protective surface
It carries the skin's blood supply
questions.why: The stratum basale holds stem cells that divide to produce new keratinocytes. When it survives an injury, these cells can repopulate all the layers above it. If the basale is destroyed over a large area along with the follicles and glands, there is no source of new epidermis, and a graft is needed.
notes: Correct. The basale's dividing cells rebuild the epidermis.
Water loss is limited by the sealant from lamellar granules in the upper epidermis, and the basale does not store water. Students choose this when they confuse barrier functions with regeneration.
The dead protective surface is the stratum corneum, at the opposite end of the epidermis. Pick the corneum if the question asked which stratum is shed and replaced.
The skin's blood supply lies in the dermis, and the basale, like the rest of the epidermis, is avascular. Choose the dermis if the question asked which layer feeds the epidermis.
questions.answerText: It holds the dividing cells that rebuild the epidermis

questions.q: Which order lists injection routes from the shallowest to the deepest tissue they reach?
questions.why: Each route is named for the layer it reaches. Intradermal places fluid within the dermis, subcutaneous places it in the hypodermis beneath the skin, and intramuscular places it in skeletal muscle deep to the hypodermis. The order of the routes matches the order of the layers: dermis, hypodermis, muscle.
notes: Correct. Intradermal, subcutaneous, intramuscular runs from shallow to deep.
This is the correct order run backward, from deepest to shallowest. It would be the answer if the question asked for the routes from deep to shallow.
This order puts subcutaneous first, but the hypodermis lies beneath the dermis, so intradermal is shallower. Students choose it when they read sub as meaning just under the epidermis.
This order places intramuscular above subcutaneous, but muscle lies deep to the hypodermis. It would only be right if muscle sat between the dermis and the fatty layer, which it does not.

questions.q: A full-thickness burn destroys the stratum basale, the hair follicles, and the sweat glands across a wide area. Why does this injury usually need a skin graft?
options: The graft is needed only to restore normal skin color
No living epidermal cells remain to regrow the epidermis
The dermis cannot survive without the epidermis above it
The hypodermis must be replaced before any healing can begin
questions.why: New epidermis can come only from living epidermal cells, either in the stratum basale or in the linings of hair follicles and sweat glands. A full-thickness burn destroys all of these, so the wound has no source of new epidermis. A graft, a patch of healthy skin moved from a donor site, supplies that missing epidermis and protects against fluid loss and infection.
notes: Skin grafts protect against fluid loss and infection, reduce scarring, and preserve function, so color is a minor benefit. This choice reflects a misconception that grafting is mainly cosmetic.
Correct. With the basale, follicles, and glands gone, nothing remains to regrow the epidermis.

In this burn the dermis itself has been destroyed, so its survival is not the issue. Students choose this because the dermis does feed the epidermis, but here the problem is the lost source of new cells.
The hypodermis is not part of the skin and does not have to be rebuilt first. Choose the hypodermis if the question asked which layer stores fat beneath the skin.
questions.answerText: No living epidermal cells remain to regrow the epidermis

questions.q: The epidermis has no blood vessels, yet its deepest cells are alive while its surface cells are dead. What explains the difference?
options: Deep cells are fed directly by vessels of the hypodermis
Deep cells sit near dermal capillaries and get nutrients by diffusion
Surface cells had their own blood vessels that later closed off
Surface cells are killed each day by direct sunlight exposure
questions.why: Because the epidermis is avascular, every living epidermal cell depends on nutrients diffusing up from capillaries in the dermis. Cells in the deepest strata are close to that supply, but as they are pushed toward the surface they get farther away, fill with keratin, and die. The dead, keratin-filled surface layer then serves as the skin's tough barrier.
notes: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and does not feed the epidermis directly. The dermis would be the answer for the layer whose capillaries nourish the epidermis.
Correct. Distance from the dermal capillaries decides which epidermal cells stay alive.
No part of the epidermis has blood vessels at any stage. Students choose this when they forget that the whole epidermis is avascular.
