Sunlight can damage skin cells, but the surface cells die as part of normal maturation even in skin that never sees the sun. This choice reflects a misconception that the dead layer is sun damage.
questions.answerText: Deep cells sit near dermal capillaries and get nutrients by diffusion

questions.q: A burn that destroys the full dermis heals with scar tissue that has no hair and no sweat glands, while a shallow scrape heals with both. Why does depth matter?
options: Hair follicles and sweat glands sit in the dermis, so destroying the dermis removes them
Hair follicles and sweat glands sit in the epidermis, so any scrape removes them
Depth does not matter, and the difference comes from the heat of the burn alone
Scar tissue grows from the hypodermis, which cannot make glands
questions.why: Hair follicles and sweat glands begin as downgrowths of the epidermis but sit deep in the dermis. A shallow scrape leaves them intact, so they remain and also help rebuild the surface. A burn that destroys the whole dermis destroys these structures too, and the scar that fills the wound cannot rebuild them.
notes: Correct. Destroying the dermis destroys the follicles and glands within it.

Follicles and glands extend deep into the dermis, which is why a shallow scrape leaves them behind. Students choose this because these structures develop from the epidermis, but they live in the dermis.
Depth is the deciding factor, since it determines whether the follicles and glands survive. This choice reflects the misconception that heat alone, not the layer reached, sets the outcome.
Scar tissue forms from connective tissue in the wound, and the hypodermis is not the source. Choose the hypodermis if the question asked which layer anchors the skin to the fascia.
questions.answerText: Hair follicles and sweat glands sit in the dermis, so destroying the dermis removes them

questions.q: Inside a keratinocyte, melanin granules gather over the side of the nucleus that faces the skin surface. What does this placement accomplish?
options: It shields the nuclear DNA from UV light
It toughens the cell against abrasion
It waterproofs the cell against water loss
It alerts immune cells to invading microbes
questions.why: Melanocytes pass melanin granules to keratinocytes, where the granules cluster into a protective veil over the surface-facing side of the nucleus. Melanin absorbs ultraviolet light, so the veil blocks UV rays before they can damage the DNA. Melanocytes themselves remain vulnerable to UV damage, since they protect other cells rather than themselves.
notes: Correct. The melanin veil absorbs UV light before it reaches the DNA.
Toughness against abrasion comes from keratin, the fibrous protein that fills keratinocytes. It would be the answer for the main protective role of keratin.
Waterproofing comes from the sealant released by lamellar granules, which keratinocytes also make. Pick waterproofing if the question asked what lamellar granules do.
Alerting the immune system is the job of intraepidermal macrophages (Langerhans cells). Choose this if the question asked which epidermal cell responds to invading microbes.
questions.answerText: It shields the nuclear DNA from UV light

questions.q: When the body overheats, which pair of skin responses helps lower body temperature?
options: Sweat production increases and dermal blood vessels constrict
Arrector pili contract and dermal blood vessels constrict
Sweat production increases and dermal blood vessels dilate
Sweat production decreases and dermal blood vessels constrict
questions.why: When the body is too warm, dermal blood vessels dilate (widen) and bring warm blood close to the surface, where heat is lost to the environment. At the same time, sweat production increases, and evaporation of sweat cools the surface. Both responses aim to shed heat.
notes: More sweat helps cool the body, but constricted vessels keep warm blood away from the surface and hold heat in. Students choose this when they remember only half of the heat-loss response.
Arrector pili contraction and vessel constriction go with being cold, producing goose bumps and keeping blood in the core. This would fit a question about responses to a chilly room.
Correct. More sweat and wider dermal vessels both release heat.
Less sweat and narrower vessels conserve heat, which is the skin's response to cold. Pick this pair if the question asked how the skin responds when the body is too cold.
questions.answerText: Sweat production increases and dermal blood vessels dilate

questions.q: Thick skin on the palms and soles has a stratum lucidum and a much thicker stratum corneum. Why is this build found there?
options: They face constant friction, and extra keratin layers resist wear
They absorb water, and extra layers draw water inward
They have the most melanocytes, and extra layers store the pigment
They hold more hair follicles, and extra layers anchor the hairs
questions.why: The palms, soles, and fingertips are the areas of greatest friction and pressure. The biggest contributor to epidermal thickness is an increased number of layers in the stratum corneum, which builds up in response to mechanical stress. These extra dead, keratin-filled layers protect the living tissue beneath.
notes: Correct. Extra keratinized layers protect surfaces that take constant friction and pressure.
Keratin and the lamellar granule sealant limit water movement through the skin rather than drawing it in. This choice reflects a misconception that skin layers soak up water.
Melanocytes are most numerous in darker areas such as the nipples, areolae, and face, not the palms and soles. Choose the areolae if the question asked where melanocytes are especially numerous.
Thick skin has no hair follicles at all. Students choose this when they assume thicker skin must hold more structures; hair follicles would be the answer for a feature of thin skin.
questions.answerText: They face constant friction, and extra keratin layers resist wear

questions.q: A patient's nail beds and lips look bluish (cyanosis) because their blood is low in oxygen. Why does low oxygen change the visible color?
options: Melanocytes make a blue pigment when oxygen drops
Oxygen-poor hemoglobin looks bluish and shows through thin tissue
Carotene in the hypodermis turns blue when oxygen drops
The stratum corneum thickens and scatters blue light when oxygen drops
questions.why: Skin color includes a pink to red tone from hemoglobin in the dermal capillaries, and that tone depends on how much oxygen the blood carries. Blood low in oxygen looks darker and bluish, and the color shows through where tissue is thin and vessels lie near the surface. That is why cyanosis is most apparent in the nail beds, lips and other mucous membranes.
notes: Melanocytes make melanin, a yellow-red to brown-black pigment, and they do not respond to blood oxygen. Pick melanocytes if the question asked what darkens skin after sun exposure.
Correct. Oxygen-poor hemoglobin looks bluish and shows through thin tissue.
Carotene is a yellow-orange pigment that does not change color with oxygen. It would be the answer if the question asked which pigment gives skin a yellowish tone from diet.
The stratum corneum thickens with friction, not with low oxygen. This choice reflects a guess that the color comes from the surface rather than from blood below it.
questions.answerText: Oxygen-poor hemoglobin looks bluish and shows through thin tissue

questions.q: When a dehydrated patient's skin is pinched, it stays tented instead of springing back. Which explanation fits?
options: The hypodermis has gained extra fat that holds the fold
The dermis has lost tissue fluid, so it is less plump and recoils poorly
The melanocytes have stopped making pigment
The stratum corneum has dried out and locks the skin in place
questions.why: The dermis is a connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibers that let skin stretch and recoil. When the body is well hydrated, the dermis is full of tissue fluid and pinched skin springs back quickly. In dehydration, the dermis loses fluid, so a pinched fold returns slowly or stays tented.
notes: Dehydration does not add fat, and the hypodermis is not what makes the skin spring back. Choose the hypodermis if the question asked which layer stores fat.
Correct. Loss of dermal fluid makes the skin slow to recoil.
Pigment production has nothing to do with skin recoil. Melanocytes would be the answer if the question asked why skin tans after UV exposure.
The stratum corneum is a thin layer of dead cells and cannot hold a fold of skin in place. Students choose it because dry skin and dehydration sound alike, but the recoil comes from the dermis.
questions.answerText: The dermis has lost tissue fluid, so it is less plump and recoils poorly

questions.q: Why is most of the nail body pink while its free edge looks white?
options: The free edge is made of a different, softer keratin
Melanocytes beneath the free edge bleach the nail
Capillaries lie under the nail body but not the free edge
The nail body contains a pink pigment that the free edge lacks
questions.why: The nail body is clear, hard keratin, and it looks pink because the vascular tissue beneath it shows through. The free edge extends past the fingertip, so no capillaries lie under it and it looks white. The lunula looks whitish for a related reason: the epithelium beneath it is thickened, so the vessels do not show.
notes: The nail body and free edge are the same hard keratin; only what lies beneath them differs. Pick a difference in keratin if the question asked how the nail body differs from the stratum corneum, since the nail holds a harder keratin and is not shed.
Melanocytes make pigment rather than bleach it, and they do not explain the white free edge. Choose melanocytes if the question asked which cells make the pigment for skin and hair color.
Correct. Blood vessels under the nail body make it pink, and the free edge has none beneath it.
The nail has no pink pigment of its own; the color comes from blood beneath it. Students choose this when they assume color must come from pigment rather than blood showing through.
questions.answerText: Capillaries lie under the nail body but not the free edge

questions.q: On a cold day, goose bumps appear on a person's forearm but never on the palm of the hand. Why?
options: The palm is thick skin, which has no hair follicles or arrector pili
The palm's arrector pili are skeletal muscle and need a conscious command
The palm has extra sweat glands that keep it warm
The palm has a stratum lucidum that blocks muscle contraction
questions.why: Goose bumps form when arrector pili, small smooth muscles attached to hair follicles, contract and pull the hairs upright. Thick skin of the palms and soles has no hair follicles and therefore no arrector pili. With nothing to contract, goose bumps cannot form there, while hairy thin skin like the forearm shows them readily.
notes: Correct. Without follicles and arrector pili, thick skin cannot form goose bumps.

Arrector pili are smooth muscle that contracts involuntarily, and the palm has none at all. Skeletal muscle would be the answer for muscle you move on purpose, such as the muscles that close the hand.
Sweat glands help cool the body, not warm it, and they are not involved in goose bumps. Eccrine glands would be the answer for which glands are especially numerous in palm skin.
The stratum lucidum is a clear epidermal layer and has no effect on muscle. Pick it if the question asked which stratum appears only in thick skin.
questions.answerText: The palm is thick skin, which has no hair follicles or arrector pili

questions.q: Which cell in the dermis engulfs bacteria and viruses that get past the defenses of the epidermis?
questions.why: The dermis contains a few macrophages, phagocytes that engulf bacteria, viruses, and debris that get past the epidermis. They are a second line of skin defense behind the intraepidermal macrophages of the epidermis. The other cells of the dermis are fibroblasts, which make fibers, and a few adipocytes near the subcutaneous layer.
notes: Adipocytes are fat cells found near the boundary with the subcutaneous layer. They would be the answer for the cells that store fat.
Correct. Dermal macrophages engulf microbes that reach the dermis.

Intraepidermal macrophages (Langerhans cells) also defend the skin, but they live in the epidermis, not the dermis, and mainly alert the immune system to invaders. Choose them if the question asked which immune cell sits in the epidermis.
Fibroblasts are the main cells of the dermis and make its collagen and elastic fibers. Pick them if the question asked which cells build the dermal fibers.

questions.q: A skin slide shows keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on top, dense irregular connective tissue below it, and a deep zone of large fat-filled cells. A pin sits in the fat zone. What is pinned, and is it part of the skin?
options: The dermis, which is part of the skin.
The hypodermis, which is the deepest layer of the skin.
The hypodermis, which is not part of the skin.
The epidermis, which is part of the skin.
questions.why: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and the dermis below it is dense irregular connective tissue. Under them lies the hypodermis, the subcutaneous layer of areolar and adipose tissue. The skin itself is only the epidermis and the dermis, so the hypodermis is not part of it.
notes: The dermis is the dense irregular connective tissue layer above the fat zone. It is part of the skin, but it is not where the pin sits.
Hypodermis is the right layer, but the skin has only two layers, the epidermis and the dermis. The hypodermis lies beneath the skin.
Correct. The fat zone is the hypodermis, which lies beneath the skin and is not part of it.
The epidermis is the keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on top, the shallowest layer, not the deep fat zone.
questions.answerText: The hypodermis, which is not part of the skin.

questions.q: A splinter passes through the epidermis and stops in the dense irregular connective tissue beneath it. Which layer has it reached, and would you expect it to bleed?
options: The dermis, and yes, because the dermis holds blood vessels.
The dermis, and no, because the dermis has no blood vessels.
The hypodermis, and yes, because it holds large blood vessels.
The epidermis, and no, because the epidermis is avascular.
questions.why: The dense irregular connective tissue just beneath the epidermis is the dermis. The epidermis is avascular, but the dermis holds the blood vessels, nerves, and glands. A splinter that reaches the dermis can draw blood.
notes: Correct. Dense irregular connective tissue under the epidermis is the dermis, which has blood vessels.
The dermis is right, but it is vascular. The layer with no blood vessels is the epidermis above it.
The hypodermis is deeper, made of areolar and adipose tissue, not dense irregular connective tissue. The splinter stopped above it.
The splinter has already passed through the epidermis. The epidermis is avascular, which is why a cut that stays in it does not bleed.
questions.answerText: The dermis, and yes, because the dermis holds blood vessels.
